title: The settings and the keys you can change
summary: The options in Supermarket Simulator are a system of their own: the game keeps a settings manager, a container and the data behind them, with separate entries for each setting and a rebinding interface for keys.
body: The options are a system of their own rather than a screen with buttons on it. The game keeps a settings manager, a container that holds the settings and the data behind them, which is why a change survives being closed and reopened.
The menu is grouped. There is a manager for the settings menu and a canvas for a category, so the list is built from categories instead of being one long page of switches.

Each setting is an entry of its own. That is what allows the game to build a list of settings where every item carries its own label and its own value, rather than every option being written out by hand.
Keys can be rebound. There is a manager, a loader and a settings object for key bindings, so the keys are data the game reads rather than names fixed in the code.

The rebinding interface is built from parts: a view for an entry, a view for a tab and a bridge that joins them. That is how one system can show keys for a controller and for a keyboard without being written twice.

The camera has settings of its own, with a listener that reacts to how wide the view is. Keeping a listener rather than setting the value directly is how a change can be picked up by everything that has to follow it.

Language is handled by a localisation manager. What gets translated is not only text: strings, sprites, audio clips and materials all have localised forms, so a picture or a sound can change with the language as well as a word.
The region can be chosen as well. There is a controller for it, a record describing a region and a localised dropdown, which is why the list of regions follows the language you are using.
The screens are assembled from panels. The build keeps a settings panel of its own, which is why what you change options on is a piece of the menu rather than the whole page.
What this entry does not tell you: which settings each platform offers, what the defaults are, or what values they take. We have not verified those, so we do not print them.

facts.claim: The game keeps a settings manager, a container for settings and the data behind them.
The settings menu is managed and grouped by category.
An individual setting is an entry of its own.
Keys can be rebound, with a manager, a loader and a settings object.
The rebinding interface is built from an entry view, a tab view and a bridge.
The camera has settings of its own with a listener that reacts to how wide the view is.
Language is handled by a localisation manager, and the game localises assets by type rather than only text.
facts.evidence: identifiers: LocalizationManager, LocalizedString, LocalizedSprite, LocalizedAudioClip, LocalizedMaterial

facts.claim: The region can be chosen, with a controller, a record for a region and a localised dropdown.
The settings menu the game draws is a picture of its own, showing the gameplay tab and rows such as enabling shoplifters.
The build keeps a settings panel of its own.
The build names its settings tabs and the buttons beside them, including a crosshair tab button.
facts.evidence: asset names: Gameplay Tab Button, Graphics Tab Button, Audio Tab Button, CrosshairTabButton

facts.claim: The build names toggles of its own for v-sync, for full screen and for confining the cursor.
facts.evidence: asset names: VSync Toggle, Full Screen Toggle, CursorConfineToggle
